Sedimentary rocks form when grains settle and become compacted or cemented. Rivers carry sand and silt toward lower ground, while wind moves fine material across exposed surfaces. The speed of flowing water affects which grains remain suspended and which collect on the bed. Coarse gravel often settles near a strong current, and fine clay can travel much farther before settling. Layers may retain ripples, impressions, or fragments of older material. Burial can reduce the spaces between grains as overlying sediment adds weight. Dissolved minerals can precipitate in those spaces and bind neighboring grains together. Different minerals respond differently to weathering at the surface. Quartz commonly survives transport that breaks down less resistant minerals. Limestone can contain shells or other remains from organisms that lived in shallow seas. Sandstone often preserves evidence of beaches, river channels, or dunes. Mudstone can form in quieter water where fine particles accumulate. Changes in color may reflect mineral composition or chemical conditions during burial. Rock exposed at the surface can crack as temperatures change or water freezes within small openings. Roots can widen cracks, and flowing water can carry loose fragments away. Mountain building can lift buried layers and expose them to erosion again. Geological maps describe the distribution of rock units at the surface.
